story: Ise-Shima is two landscapes joined by the people who use them. Inland, wooded hills around the upper Isuzu River rise behind Ise Jingū. On the coast the Shima Peninsula breaks into a ria shore of drowned valleys, so that Ago Bay and Gokasho Bay are mazes of inlets, headlands and small wooded islands, their calm water facing the open Pacific. The warm Kuroshio current runs offshore and keeps the climate mild. Evergreen broadleaf forest covers the hills, and in the shallows grow forests of kajime and arame kelp that shelter abalone, turban shells and spiny lobster.

Ise Jingū is a family of 125 shrines centred on two, the Inner Shrine (Naikū), dedicated to Amaterasu, and the Outer Shrine (Gekū). Since 690 the main sanctuaries have been rebuilt on a neighbouring plot every twenty years in the Shikinen Sengū; the 62nd rebuilding was completed in 2013, and the rites of the 63rd began in 2025. The hills behind the Inner Shrine have been the shrine's forest for some 1,300 years. The woods around the sanctuaries are never cut. The rest is worked, and since 1923 the shrine has been growing hinoki cypress on a 200-year plan, so that one day it can again supply its own timber.

People here have always lived from the sea. Shima was a miketsukuni, a province that sent seafood to the imperial court and the shrine, and Toba and Shima still have more ama than anywhere else in Japan: women who dive without breathing gear for abalone and turban shells, warm themselves in huts on the shore, and fish under old rules that spare small abalone and limit diving days. In 1893 Mikimoto Kōkichi produced the first cultured pearls, half-round ones, on Ojima, a small island off Toba. Pearl farming spread through Ago Bay, and its rafts are now as much a part of the view as the islands.

The national park was designated on 20 November 1946, the first created in Japan after the Second World War, and it was drawn round people rather than wilderness. More than 96 per cent of its land is privately owned and a large population lives inside it. What it protects is a working landscape: satoyama hills of fields, villages and woodland, and satoumi bays of rafts, harbours and kelp beds, kept in shape by the farming, fishing and forestry that made them.
howItWorks: Ise-Shima is a park of private land. Of its 55,544 hectares, more than 96 per cent is privately owned and only 165 hectares belong to the state, and the cities of Ise, Toba and Shima and the town of Minami-Ise all lie partly within it. Even the strictest zone is private. The special protection zone, about 1,000 hectares, is mostly Ise Jingū's sacred precinct and part of its forest, kept for its natural warm-temperate evergreen woodland; the rest is a handful of headlands and islets on the Minami-Ise coast, among them Mieshima, whose sea caves shelter wintering house martins.

About two-thirds of the land is ordinary zone, where large buildings and earthworks must be notified but farming, fishing and village life carry on. In the special zones, which take in the shrine forest, Futami-ura, Kamishima's Benten cape and the finest natural coast, building, felling and reclaiming land need permission, and designated plants may not be picked. At sea the park covers some 20,900 hectares, all ordinary zone; there is no marine park zone. Fishing rights belong to the local fishing co-operatives, and taking abalone, turban shells, sea cucumber or spiny lobster without them is poaching, punished with heavy fines.

Ise Jingū sets its own rules. Pets cannot be taken in (they can be left at the guard posts at the entrances), and visitors are asked not to eat or smoke on the approaches; smoking is allowed only at the designated spots. Drones, tripods for long sessions, stepladders, live-streaming and commercial filming are refused, and photography is forbidden where signs say so. Keep left at the Outer Shrine and right at the Inner. On the Shima coast, two beaches where loggerhead turtles nest, Hiyorihama–Sangūhama and Hironohama, are closed to vehicles from 1 May to 31 October.

sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-ise-jingu-inner-shrine: Amaterasu's shrine, reached over the Uji Bridge and through centuries-old trees beside the Isuzu River. Its sanctuary has been rebuilt every twenty years since 690.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-yokoyama-observatory: Ago Bay from above: a maze of drowned valleys, wooded islets and rows of pearl rafts. The park's visitor centre is close by.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-meoto-iwa-futami-ura: Two sea rocks off Futami's old purification beach, tied together by a sacred rope, with a torii on the larger. From May to July the sun rises between them.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-mount-asama: The park's highest point at 555 m. The summit observatory looks across Ise Bay and down the Shima coast, and on clear winter days to Mount Fuji.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-daiozaki-lighthouse: A lighthouse on the cape above the fishing town of Daiō, where the Kinki Nature Trail turns from the sheltered bays to the open Pacific.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-anorisaki-lighthouse: Climb it for the open Pacific on one side and a calm bay on the other. One of Japan's fifty selected lighthouses.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-mieshima-viewpoint-ugur: Over the drowned valleys of the Minami-Ise coast to a heart-shaped inlet, with tuna and pearl farms in the water below.
sightNotes.poi-jp-ise-shima-kamishima: The farthest of Toba's four inhabited islands, under one square kilometre, with white limestone karst by the sea. The setting of Yukio Mishima's novel The Sound of Waves.

planYourVisit.reservations: No booking is needed to visit Ise Jingū or the viewpoints. Ama-hut meals, diving with ama, sea-kayak tours and pearl workshops are run by local operators and are best booked ahead. Ferries and bay cruises stop in high wind and heavy seas; check timetables with the operators before you go.
permits: No permits are needed to walk or to visit the shrines
Filming for publication inside Ise Jingū needs the shrine office's permission in advance

chronology.text: The first Shikinen Sengū rebuilds Ise Jingū; the forest behind it becomes the shrine's timber hill.
Mikimoto Kōkichi produces the first cultured pearls on Ojima, off Toba.
Ise Jingū starts a 200-year plan to grow its own hinoki cypress in the shrine forest.
Ise-Shima National Park is designated on 20 November, the first national park after the Second World War.
A review creates the special protection zone and extends the park along the Minami-Ise coast.
Vehicles are banned from two turtle-nesting beaches in summer, and Yokoyama becomes a visitor facility district.
The ama fishing techniques of Toba and Shima become a national Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property.
The rites of the 63rd Shikinen Sengū begin, leading to the transfer to new sanctuaries in 2033.

safety: Toba and Shima lie where a Nankai Trough earthquake would bring a large tsunami within minutes; in 1944 waves reached the southern Mie coast 5 to 15 minutes after the shaking. On the coast, if you feel strong or long shaking or see the red-and-white chequered tsunami flag, go to high ground at once.
The outer coast at Daiōzaki, Anorisaki and the Sakishima Peninsula faces the open Pacific. Stay off wave-washed rocks in heavy seas, and keep away from the shore when a typhoon approaches.
Go sea kayaking or snorkelling with a local guide, and keep clear of the pearl and fish rafts: they are working farms, tended by boat.
Summers are hot and humid. Carry water on the coast paths and on the walk up Mount Asama.
regulations: Do not take abalone, turban shells, sea cucumber or spiny lobster: they are reserved to local fishing co-operatives or to licensed fishers, and taking them is poaching, with heavy fines. Release any spiny lobster caught by chance.
At Ise Jingū: no pets, no eating or smoking on the approaches (smoking only at the designated spots), no drones, and no photography where it is forbidden.
Vehicles are banned on the Hiyorihama–Sangūhama and Hironohama nesting beaches from 1 May to 31 October.
In the special zones, designated plants may not be picked or dug up without permission.

weather: Warmed by the Kuroshio current offshore, Ise-Shima has mild winters and long, humid summers. The rainy season runs from June into July, and typhoons can reach the coast from late summer into autumn, stopping ferries and boat trips. Spring and autumn are the easiest seasons for walking the coast and the shrine forest. From May to July the sun rises between the Meoto Iwa, and on clear winter days Mount Fuji can be seen across the sea from Mount Asama.
directions: Kintetsu limited expresses run from Osaka and Nagoya to Iseshi in under two hours, and most continue to Toba and Kashikojima; JR's rapid Mie trains run from Nagoya to Iseshi and Toba. From Tokyo, take the Tōkaidō Shinkansen to Nagoya, about 100 minutes, and change there. Mie Kōtsū buses link the two shrines with Futami, and other routes cover the peninsula. Toba City's ferries leave Toba Marine Terminal for Sakatejima, Tōshijima, Sugashima and Kamishima, and boats from Kashikojima cross Ago Bay to Mazaki and Wagu. By car, the Pearl Road follows the coast between Toba and Shima.
